I Appendix A - Cluster merging

After applying the region growing algorithm, a single continuous surface may become over-segmented into multiple clusters. To address this issue, we employ a cluster merging algorithm. In this algorithm, we first define a cluster pair (Ci,Cj)(C_{i},C_{j}), which consists of two distinct clusters. The purpose of defining such a pair is to assess whether the clusters belong to the same continuous surface by examining adjacent boundary points between them.

For each cluster pair, boundary point pairs are detected within the specified distance threshold ρd\rho_{d} as described in Alg. 1 (Step 1). In this step, the boundary status of each point is evaluated by considering k1k_{1} neighboring points and at least three boundary point pairs must be detected. If the number of boundary point pairs is less than three, the cluster pair is considered to contain noisy or unstable boundary information and is excluded from merging. Next, for each boundary point, an average normal is computed using k2k_{2} neighbors to estimate the local surface normal vector. If the dot product between the average normal vectors is at least ρn\rho_{n}, and the difference in mean curvature is below ρc\rho_{c}, the boundary points are deemed similar, indicating that the boundaries of the two clusters likely belong to the same continuous surface (Alg. 1, Step 2).

Since boundary conditions alone may not fully overcome noise or inaccuracies near the boundaries, additional reliable internal information is incorporated. As shown in Alg. 1 (Step 3), each cluster selects a representative internal point piinp_{i}^{\mathrm{in}}, which is the median point sorted by perpendicular distance to the principal axis, and the normals and curvatures of these internal points are compared using thresholds ρi​n,n\rho_{in,n} for normals and ρi​n,c\rho_{in,c} for curvatures. The clusters are merged only if both the boundary and internal conditions are satisfied. Once the conditions are met, cluster CjC_{j} is merged into CiC_{i} (Alg. 1, Step 4), and this process is repeated until no further mergers can be performed (Alg. 1, Line 28).

II Appendix B - ICP refinement

After obtaining initial candidate pairs through descriptor matching, false matches may still exist. To eliminate these, we apply the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm to iteratively optimize point-to-point or point-to-line alignments, thereby refining the local alignment between sherds.

Pairwise cost function.

JR​(A,B):=∑(i,j)∈ΩA​Bρd​(di​j​(𝚃A,𝚃B))+λ​ρe​(ei​j2​(𝚃A,𝚃B))\displaystyle J_{R}(A,B):=\sum_{\smash{\mathclap{(i,j)\in\Omega^{AB}}}}\rho_{d}(d_{ij}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B}))+\lambda\rho_{e}(e^{2}_{ij}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B})) (8)

Equation (8) encourages two sherds, AA and BB, to align their shared fracture surfaces (edge lines) by matching corresponding points. Let ΩA​B={(i,j)|𝐪iA∈A,𝐪jB∈B}\Omega^{AB}=\{(i,j)|\mathbf{q}^{A}_{i}\in A,\mathbf{q}^{B}_{j}\in B\} as the correspondence index set between sherd AA and sherd BB. Here, ρd​(⋅)\rho_{d}(\cdot) and ρe​(⋅)\rho_{e}(\cdot) are Cauchy kernels, and λ\lambda is a positive scalar that balances the weight of the normal misalignment term, which we set to 0.4 in our experiments. The function di​jd_{ij} represents the geometric error (e.g. point-to-point or point-to-line distance) between the corresponding points and ei​je_{ij} measures the squared difference between their surface normals.

At first ICP iteration, we use geometric error function as a point-to-point (P2P) alignment (di​j​(𝚃A,𝚃B)=di​jP2P​(𝚃A,𝚃B)d_{ij}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B})=d_{ij}^{\text{P2P}}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B}):

di​jP2P​(𝚃A,𝚃B)\displaystyle d_{ij}^{\mathrm{P2P}}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B}) :=d⁡(𝐩iA,𝐧^iA,𝐩jB,𝐧^jB,𝚃A,𝚃B)\displaystyle:=d(\mathbf{p}^{A}_{i},\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{p}^{B}_{j},\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{B}_{j},\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B}) (9)
=‖mi​j​(𝚃A,𝚃B)‖22\displaystyle=\bigl\|m_{ij}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B})\bigr\|_{2}^{2}
mi​j​(𝚃A,𝚃B)\displaystyle m_{ij}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B}) :=mi​j​(𝐩iA,𝐧^iA,𝐩jB,𝐧^jB,𝚃A,𝚃B)\displaystyle:=m_{ij}(\mathbf{p}^{A}_{i},\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{p}^{B}_{j},\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{B}_{j},\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B}) (10)
=𝚁A​𝐩iA+𝐭A−𝚁B​𝐩jB−𝐭B\displaystyle=\mathtt{R}^{A}\mathbf{p}^{A}_{i}+\mathbf{t}^{A}-\mathtt{R}^{B}\mathbf{p}^{B}_{j}-\mathbf{t}^{B}

where 𝚁A,𝚁B∈ℝ3×3\mathtt{R}^{A},\mathtt{R}^{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} are rotation matrices that transform sherds AA and BB, 𝐭A,𝐭B∈ℝ3\mathbf{t}^{A},\mathbf{t}^{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} are translation vectors, and 𝐩iA,𝐩jB\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A},\mathbf{p}_{j}^{B} are points on each sherd’s edge line.

Once the sherds have been roughly aligned after the first iteration of ICP, we switch the P2P alignment to point-to-line (P2L) alignment. Empirically, P2P model often adjusts precise geometric difference under good initial condition. Specifically,

di​jP2L​(TA,TB):=d⁡(𝐩iA,𝐧^iA,𝐩jB,𝐧^jB,𝚃A,𝚃B)\displaystyle d_{ij}^{\mathrm{P2L}}(T_{A},T_{B}):=d(\mathbf{p}^{A}_{i},\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{p}^{B}_{j},\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{B}_{j},\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B}) (11)
=‖𝚁A​𝐥^iA⋅mi​j​(𝚃A,𝚃B)‖22+‖𝚁B​𝐥^jB⋅mi​j​(𝚃A,𝚃B)‖22\displaystyle=\bigl\|\mathtt{R}^{A}\hat{\mathbf{l}}_{i}^{A}\cdot m_{ij}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B})\bigr\|_{2}^{2}+\bigl\|\mathtt{R}^{B}\hat{\mathbf{l}}_{j}^{B}\cdot m_{ij}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B})\bigr\|_{2}^{2}
+‖𝚁A​𝐧^iA⋅mi​j​(𝚃A,𝚃B)‖22+‖𝚁B​𝐧^jB⋅mi​j​(𝚃A,𝚃B)‖22\displaystyle+\bigl\|\mathtt{R}^{A}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}^{A}\cdot m_{ij}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B})\bigr\|_{2}^{2}+\bigl\|\mathtt{R}^{B}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{j}^{B}\cdot m_{ij}(\mathtt{T}^{A},\mathtt{T}^{B})\bigr\|_{2}^{2}

where 𝐥^iA\hat{\mathbf{l}}_{i}^{A} denotes the fracture surface normal of the edge line on sherd AA. To clarify, the fracture surface normal (𝐥^i\hat{\mathbf{l}}_{i}) of an edge line point is distinct from its the surface normal (𝐧^i\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}). Specifically, the fracture surface normal (𝐥^i\hat{\mathbf{l}}_{i}) is a normalized vector orthogonal to the local fracture surface of the edge line point 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i}. It can be computed by taking the cross product between the point’s surface normal (𝐧^i\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}) and the tangent vector:

𝐥^iA:=𝐧^iA×(𝐩i+1A−𝐩iA)‖𝐧^iA×(𝐩i+1A−𝐩iA)‖2\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{l}}_{i}^{A}~:=~\frac{\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}^{A}\,\times\,\bigl(\mathbf{p}_{i+1}^{A}-\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}\bigr)}{\bigl\|\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}^{A}\,\times\,\bigl(\mathbf{p}_{i+1}^{A}-\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}\bigr)\bigr\|_{2}} (12)

This distinction resolves the local minima caused by simple geometric characteristic of ceramic broken sherds. Because it ensures that the fracture surface normal is orthogonal to the local surface geometry of the fracture edge, aiding in alignment accuracy during optimization, as shown in Fig. 9 in main paper.

ei​j​(TA,TB):=‖RA​n^iA−RB​n^jB‖22\displaystyle e_{ij}(T_{A},\,T_{B})~:=~\bigl\|\,R_{A}\,\hat{n}_{i}^{A}~-~R_{B}\,\hat{n}_{j}^{B}\bigr\|_{2}^{2} (13)

Equation (13) ensures the surface normals of the two sherds remain consistent when they are matched.

Individual cost function.

JI​(A):=μ​∑i∈ΩAρf​(fi2​(𝚃A))+ν​∑i∈ΨAρg​(gi2​(𝚃A,rrim,hrim))\displaystyle J_{I}(A):=\mu\!\!\sum_{i\in\Omega_{A}}\!\!\rho_{f}\big(f_{i}^{2}(\mathtt{T}^{A})\big)+\nu\!\!\sum_{i\in\Psi_{A}}\!\!\rho_{g}\big(g_{i}^{2}(\mathtt{T}^{A},r^{\mathrm{rim}},h^{\mathrm{rim}})\big) (14)

where ΩA\Omega_{A} is the set of points used for axis alignment, and ΨA\Psi_{A} is the set of rim points (e.g., the top edge of the pottery). μ\mu and ν\nu is a positive scalar that balance the weight of the axis alignment term and the rim-consistency term, respectively, both of which we set to 0.4 in our experiments. fif_{i} aligns each sherd to the global symmetry axis, extending the geometric error approach proposed by Cao and Mumford [1] and further developed in PotSAC [7]. This method robustly handles the normal sign ambiguity for inner and outer surfaces by considering both inward and outward normals. Specifically, the deviation of the curvature center from the symmetry axis can be measured as:

ϵis​(𝐮,𝐯^):=(cis​(𝐮,𝐯^)−𝐮)×𝐯^\displaystyle\epsilon_{i}^{s}(\mathbf{u},\hat{\mathbf{v}}):=\bigl(c_{i}^{s}(\mathbf{u},\hat{\mathbf{v}})-\mathbf{u}\bigr)\times\hat{\mathbf{v}} (15)
cis​(𝐮,𝐯^):=𝐩i−‖(𝐩i−𝐮)×𝐯^‖2‖𝐯^×𝐧^is‖2​𝐧^is\displaystyle c_{i}^{s}(\mathbf{u},\hat{\mathbf{v}}):=\mathbf{p}_{i}-\frac{\|(\mathbf{p}_{i}-\mathbf{u})\times\hat{\mathbf{v}}\|_{2}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}\times\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}^{s}\|_{2}}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}^{s}

where s∈{+,−}s\in\{+,-\} indicates the normal direction (inward or outward), 𝐯^\hat{\mathbf{v}} and 𝐮\mathbf{u} are the direction and offset of the symmetric axis, respectively. To account for this ambiguity, a log-sum-exp smoothing function is applied:

fi:=−1t​ln⁡(∑sexp⁡(−t​‖ϵis‖22))\displaystyle f_{i}:=-\tfrac{1}{t}\ln\left(\sum_{s}\exp\Big(-t\,\|\epsilon_{i}^{s}\|_{2}^{2}\Big)\right) (16)

where ‖ϵi+‖2\|\epsilon_{i}^{+}\|^{2} and ‖ϵi−‖2\|\epsilon_{i}^{-}\|^{2} represent the squared deviations for inward and outward normals, respectively. This approach ensures robust alignment of sherds to the global symmetry axis, even in cases where the normal directions are flipped.

The rim-consistency term gig_{i} enforces that the points belonging to the rim adhere to rim constraints. Specifically,

gi​(𝚃A,rrim,hrim)=\displaystyle g_{i}(\mathtt{T}^{A},r^{\mathrm{rim}},h^{\mathrm{rim}})= ‖rrim−r⁡(RA​piA+tA)‖22\displaystyle\bigl\|\,r^{\mathrm{rim}}-r\bigl(R^{A}\,p_{i}^{A}+t^{A}\bigr)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}
+‖hrim−h⁡(RA​piA+tA)‖22\displaystyle+\bigl\|\,h^{\mathrm{rim}}-h\bigl(R^{A}\,p_{i}^{A}+t^{A}\bigr)\bigr\|_{2}^{2} (17)

where rrimr^{\mathrm{rim}} and hrimh^{\mathrm{rim}} are radius and height of rim based on axis of symmetric, computed as the median value of all rim points. The function r⁡(𝐩)r(\mathbf{p}) and h⁡(𝐩)h(\mathbf{p}) compute radius and height of 𝐩\mathbf{p}, respectively. This constraints ensures that all rim points lie on the same circular lip after transformation.

III Appendix C - Geometric verification

To ensure the accurate reassembly of pottery fragments, it is essential to verify whether the edge lines of the fragments align correctly. This process involves two key steps: overlap checking (Algorithm 2) and profile curve consistency verification (Algorithm 3).

Checking potential overlaps.   The overlap check identifies corresponding edge points between two fragments and evaluates their potential overlap in 3D space. The two conditions with asterisks (*) in Algorithm 2 are designed to select the potential overlapping regions:

  1. 1.

    ‖𝐩jA−𝐩jB‖2<d\left\lVert\mathbf{p}_{j}^{A}-\mathbf{p}_{j}^{B}\right\rVert_{2}<d

  2. 2.

    𝐧jA⋅𝐧jB>0\mathbf{n}_{j}^{A}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{j}^{B}>0 and |(𝐩jA−𝐩jB)‖𝐩jA−𝐩jB‖2⋅𝐧jA|>cos⁡θ\left|\frac{(\mathbf{p}_{j}^{A}-\mathbf{p}_{j}^{B})}{\|\mathbf{p}_{j}^{A}-\mathbf{p}_{j}^{B}\|_{2}}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{j}^{A}\right|>\cos\theta

The first condition filters out candidate points by measuring their Euclidean distance, ensuring that only closely aligned points are considered. The second condition examines the possible overlapping alongside the radial direction as shown in Fig 1. Once the region of interest is detected, we further verify additional conditions (†\dagger). First, whether one fragment is partially embedded inside another (𝐥^jA⋅𝐥^jB>0)\big(\hat{\mathbf{l}}_{j}^{A}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{l}}_{j}^{B}>0\big). This occurs when one piece is almost submerged into another piece. Second, when two fragments overlap in an unexpected manner (𝐥^jA⋅(𝐩jB−𝐩jA)<0CLOSE\big(\hat{\mathbf{l}}_{j}^{A}\cdot(\mathbf{p}_{j}^{B}-\mathbf{p}_{j}^{A})<0 and OPEN𝐥^jB⋅(𝐩jB−𝐩jA)>0)\hat{\mathbf{l}}_{j}^{B}\cdot(\mathbf{p}_{j}^{B}-\mathbf{p}_{j}^{A})>0\big). This occurs when two pieces match as expected but with some overlaps. If the total overlapped area So​v​e​r​l​a​pS_{overlap} exceeds 50​mm250\text{mm}^{2}, the pair is discarded from the match list.

Checking the profile curve.   However, overlap checking alone cannot eliminate all false positive matches, necessitating an additional profile curve consistency verification step. The profile curve represents the projection of the pot’s edge onto the r​zrz-plane, reflecting its axial symmetry. A correctly assembled pot should exhibit a continuous, smooth profile curve. To evaluate this, the edge points are first aligned to the symmetry axis, and their radial distances are computed. The points are then segmented into bins at 7​mm7\text{mm} intervals along the zz-axis, and within each bin, a line is fitted using orthogonal regression. The standard deviation of the orthogonal distance errors between the fitted line and the actual edge points is then measured. If this deviation exceeds a predefined threshold 7​mm7\text{mm}, the match is deemed inconsistent and rejected.

By integrating both verification methods, the algorithm effectively reduces errors that may arise from purely distance-based matching. Fig. 1 illustrates an example of a detected radial overlap, while Fig. 2 demonstrates a case where the overlap test fails to identify a false positive configuration, but the profile curve consistency check successfully detects the mismatch. The combination of these two algorithms significantly enhances the reliability and accuracy of pottery fragment reassembly.

IV Appendix D - Additional experimental visualization of reassembly

We present a visual comparison of reassembly results corresponding to the quantitative evaluations in Tables V and VI in the main paper [44]. Fig. 3 and 4 show pottery reassembled using different methods, including Jigsaw [22], FRASIER [15], PuzzleFusion++ [39], and our proposed SfS++  (with k=5k=5, b=3b=3). Each row depicts a pot reconstructed from 2 to 20 fragments, aligning with the fragment range used during training for deep learning-based models. The first column provides ground truth models for reference, while the last column presents the results of our method, demonstrating improved reassembly quality over existing approaches.
